la:verb:peto.gloss: to ask, beg, request, look for, inquire, petition, entreat
senses: to ask, beg, request, look for, inquire, petition, entreat
to attack, to assail, to thrust at
to aim at (with the person attacked in the accusative and the weapon/projectile in the ablative)
to missionize or proselytize among the people of a place
la:verb:peto.html:
pĕto, īvi and ĭi, ītum, 3 (
perf. petīt, ; Ov F. 1, 109: petisti,; ; : petistis,: petissem,; ; : petisse,; ; Ov.

M. 9, 623; cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, 516 sq.), v. a.

Sanscr. root pat-, to fall upon, fly, find; Gr. πετ- in πίπτω (πι-πέτω), to fall; cf. Lat. impetus and in πέτομαι, to fly; cf. Lat. penna, acci-pit-er, etc.; the root of πίπτω, and therefore orig. to fall, fall upon; hence, to endeavor to reach or attain any thing
.

To fall upon any thing.
Lit.
In a hostile sense, to rush at, attack, assault, assail; to let fly at, aim a blow at, thrust at, etc. (class.; cf.: invado, aggredior): gladiatores et vitando caute, et petendo vehementer,: cujus latus mucro ille petebat,: non latus aut ventrem, sed caput et collum petere,to thrust at,: aliquem spiculo infeste,: aliquem mālo,to throw an apple at any one,: alicui ungue genas,: aliquem saxis, id. de Nuce, 2: aprum jaculis,: aëra disco,: bello Penatìs,: armis patriam,.—
Without the notion of hostility: petere collum alicujus amplexu, to fall upon one's neck, to embrace one, M. Cael. ap. .—Esp. freq., to seek, to direct one's course to, to go or repair to, to make for, travel to a place: grues loca calidiora petentes,: Cyzicum,: Dyrrhachium,: naves,to seek, take refuge in their ships,: caelum pennis,to fly,: Graiis Phasi petite viris,visited by the Greeks,: Metellus Postumium ad bellum gerendum Africam petentem, ... urbem egredi passus non est,attempting to go, starting,.—Transf., of things, to proceed or go towards: campum petit amnis,: mons petit astra,towers toward the stars,: aliquem, to seek, go to a person: reginam,: ut te supplex peterem, et tua limina adirem,: aliquid in locum or ad aliquem, to go to a place or person for something, to go in quest of, go to fetch: visum est tanti in extremam Italiam petere Brundisium ostreas,to go to Brundisium for oysters,: myrrham ad Troglodytas,: harena ad Aethiopas usque petitur,: collis, in quem vimina petebantur,: quaeque trans maria petimus,fetch,, §§ 58, 52.—
Trop.
To attack, assail one with any thing (class.): aiiquem epistulā,: aliquem fraude et insidiis,: aliquem falsis criminibus,.—
To demand, seek, require (cf. posco).
In gen.: ita petit asparagus,: ex iis tantum, quantum res petet, hauriemus,: aliquem in vincula,: aliquem ad supplicium,: poenas ab aliquo, to seek satisfaction from or revenge one's self on any one. ut poenas ab optimo quoque peteret sui doloris, : ut merito ab eā poenas liberi sui petere debuerint,.—
In partic.
To demand or claim at law, to bring an action to recover, to sue for any thing (syn.: postulo): causam dicere Prius unde petitur ... Quam ille qui petit,: qui per se litem contestatur, sibi soli petit,: aliquando cum servis Habiti furti egit; nuper ab ipso Habito petere coepit,: qui non calumniā litium alienos fundos, sed castris, exercitu, signis inferendis petebat,.—
To beg, beseech, ask, request, desire, entreat (syn.: rogo, flagito, obsecro); constr with ab and abl. of pers. (cf. infra); ante- and postclass., with acc. of pers.: vos volo, vos peto atque obsecro,; freq. with ut: a te etiam atque etiam peto atque contendo, ut, etc.,: peto quaesoque, ut, etc.,: peto igitur a te, vel, si pateris, oro, ut,: petere in beneficii loco et gratiae, ut,: petere precibus per litteras ab aliquo, ut,: pacem ab aliquo,: opem ab aliquo,: vitam nocenti,: petito, ut intrare urbem liceret,.—Also, with id or illud, and ut, etc.: illud autem te peto, ut, etc., Dolab. ap. .—With obj.-clause (mostly poet.): arma umeris arcumque animosa petebat Ferre,; cf.: cum peteret (solum) donari quasi proprio suo deo, : petit aes sibi dari εις ἄρτους, .—De aliquo (for ab aliquo), to beg or request of one (post-class.): si de me petisses, ut, etc.,.—Ab aliquo aliquid alicui, to beg a thing of one person for another (class.): M. Curtio tribunatum a Caesare petivi,: ab aliquo pro aliquo petere, to intercede for: in eorum studiis, qui a te pro Ligario petunt,.—With ex and abl. pers. (v. infra d.): eum petit litteris, ut ad Britanniam proficisceretur,; .—Hence, pĕtītum, i, n., a prayer, desire, request, entreaty, .—
Polit. t. t., to apply or solicit for an office, to be a candidate for office (different from ambire, to go about among the people to collect their votes, to canvass, which took place after the petitio): nemo est ex iis, qui nunc petunt, qui, etc.,: consulatum,: praeturam,; .—
To solicit a person, to seek to possess, to woo: libidine sic accensa (Sempronia) ut viros saepius peteret quam peteretur,: cum te tam multi peterent, tu me una petisti,: formosam quisque petit,: multi illam petiere,; cf.: quae tuus Vir petet, cave, ne neges; Ne petitum aliunde eat,.—
To endeavor to obtain or pursue, to seek, strive after any thing, : fugā salutem petere,: praedam pedibus,: gloriam,: eloquentiae principatum,: sanguinis profusio vel fortuita vel petita,intentional, designed, produced by artificial means,.—With inf.: bene vivere,: victricemque petunt dextrae conjungere dextram,; : conubiis natam sociare Latinis,: aliquem transfigere ferro,.—With ex and abl., over, in the case of: ex hostibus victoriam petere,: supplicium ex se, non victoriam peti,: imperium ex victis hostibus populum Romanum petere,.—
To fetch any thing: qui argentum petit,: cibum e flammā,: altius initium rei demonstrandae,: aliquid a Graecis,: a litteris exiguam doloris oblivionem,to obtain,: suspirium alte,to fetch a deep sigh,; cf.: latere petitus imo spiritus,; and: gemitus alto de corde petiti,: haec ex veteri memoriā petita,.—
To take, betake one's self to any thing: iter a Vibone Brundisium terrā petere contendi,: diversas vias,: alium cursum,to take another route,: aliam in partem petebant fugam,betook themselves to flight, fled,.—
To refer to, relate to (poet.): Trojanos haec monstra petunt,.

la:noun:petitio.html:
pĕtītĭo, ōnis, f.
peto
.
Lit., anattack, a blow, thrust, pass: tuas petiti ones effugi,; cf.: petitiones proprie dicimus impetus gladiorum,.—
Trop., an attack made in words before a court of justice, ; or in debate,; cf.: novi omnis hominis petitiones rationesque dicendi,methods of attack,; .—
In gen., a requesting, beseeching; a request, petition for any thing (postAug.), : huic quoque petitioni tuae negare non sustineo, Traj. ap. (23); —
Esp. (eccl. Lat.), a request offered to God, a prayer: impleat Dominus omnes petitiones tuas,; ; Johan. 5, 15: petitionem offerre Domino Deo, Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 16, 1, 4.—
In partic.
An applying or soliciting for office, an application, solicitation, candidacy, : petitioni se dari,to become a candidate for office,: consulatus,: pontificatūs,: regni,: tribunatūs et aedilitatis,: dare alicui petitionem consulatūs,to admit one as a candidate for the consulship,: abstinere petitione honorum,; : petitioni se dare,to solicit an office,.—
A laying claim to any thing, a suit, petition, in private or civil cases (opp. the accusatio, in criminal cases): petitio pecuniae,: hereditatis,: integram petitionem relinquere,.—
A right of claim, a right to bring an action of recovery: cavere, neminem, cujus petitio sit, petiturum,; .

la:verb:petiturio.gloss: to desire to sue for office, long to become a candidate
senses: to desire to sue for office, long to become a candidate
la:verb:petiturio.html:
pĕtītŭrio, īre,
v. desid. a. [peto], to desire to sue for office, to long to become a candidate (rare but class.): video hominem valde petiturire,.

la:other:Petelia.gloss: a city in Bruttium situated near Croton
senses: a city in Bruttium situated near Croton
la:other:Petelia.html:
Pĕtēlĭa (also Pĕtīlĭa and Pĕtellĭa), ae, f., = Πετηλία
A very ancient town in the Bruttian territory, north of Croton, colonized by Lucanians, near the mod. Strongoli, ; ; ; .—Hence,
Pĕtēlī-nus (Pĕtellīn-), a, um, adj., Petelian: Petelinus lucus, near Rome,: Petelina fides,fin.—Subst.: Pĕtēlīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Petelia, the Petelians, .—
A city on the western coast of Lucania, between Paestum and Velia, , ext. 1.—Hence,
† Pĕtēlīni, ōrum, m., the Petelians, ; .

senses: a rustic, a country bumpkin, yokel, hayseed, hick
an old wether (a ram whose flesh is as hard as stone)
la:noun:petro.html:
pē^tro, ōnis, m.
1. petra
.
A rustic: petrones rustici fere dicuntur, etc., Müll.; cf.: petrones rustici a petrarum asperitate et duritiā dicti, Paul. ex ib.—
An old wether, whose flesh is as hard as a stone (anteclass.), .

la:noun:petra.html:
pē^tra, ae, f., = πέτρα,
a rock, a crag, stone (pure Lat. saxum; cf.: rupes, scopulus): petrarum genera sunt duo, quorum alterum naturale saxum prominens in mare; alterum manufactum ut docet Aelius Gallus: Petra est, qui locus dextrā ac sinistrā fornicem expletur usque ad libramentum summi fornicis, Müll. (of the latter signif. there is no other example known): petris ingentibus tecta, Enn. ap. . 1. (Ann. v. 366); 804: aquam de petrā produxit, et saep.: gaviae in petris nidificant,: alga, quae juxta terram in petris nascitur,; ; .

la:other:Petra.gloss: Petra (an ancient Nabatean city in Arabia Petraea, in modern Jordan)
senses: Petra (an ancient Nabatean city in Arabia Petraea, in modern Jordan)
Petra, Petra in Aegypto (an ancient Hellenistic city and former bishopic in Roman Egypt)
Petra (a medieval fortified town in Lazica, in the modern country of Georgia; modern Tsikhisdziri)
Petra (an ancient lost town in Corinthia in modern Greece)
Petra (an ancient lost town in Elis in modern Greece)
a post-classical female given name, masculine equivalent Petrus

la:adj:petulans.html:
pĕtŭlans, antis, adj.
prop. part. of the obsol. petulo, from peto, qs. falling upon or assailing in jest, i. e.
,
forward, pert, saucy, impudent, wanton, freakish, petulant.
In gen. (class.; syn.: protervus, lascivus, procax): petulantes et petulci etiam appellantur, qui protervo impetu, et crebro petunt laedendi alterius gratiā, Müll.: homo,: effuse petulans,: animalia,: pictura,: petulans et furiosum genus dicendi,: Tarentum,.—Comp., .—Sup.: imitatio petulantissima,.—
In partic., wanton, lascivious (class.): si petulans fuisset in aliquā generosā nobili virgine,.— Adv.: pĕtŭlanter, pertly, wantonly, impudently, petulantly (class.): in aliquem invehi,: vivere,.—Comp.: petulantius,. —Sup.: petulantissime,.

la:noun:petulantia.html:
pĕtŭlantĭa, ae, f.
petulans
.
Lit., sauciness, freakishness, impudence, wantonness, petulance (class.; syn. lascivia): itaque a petendo petulantia, a procando, id est poscendo, procacitas nominata est, ap. : petulantia et libido magis est adulescentium quam senum,: petulantia et audacia,; cf.: te non ulla meae laesit petulantia linguae,.—In plur.: Naevius ... cum ob assiduam maledicentiam et probra in principes civitatis ... in vincula conjectus esset ... in his fabulis, delicta sua et petulantias dictorum, quibus multos ante laeserat, diluisset,insolent language, libels,.—
In a milder sense, carelessness, heedlessness (ante-class.): linguae,; .—
Transf.
Of animals, viciousness: cornuti fere perniciosi sunt propter petulantiam,.—
Of things, exuberance, luxuriance: ramorum,: morbi,violence,.

la:noun:petitor.html:
pĕtītor, ōris, m.
peto
.
In gen., a seeker, striver after any thing (poet.): famae,.—
In partic.
Polit. t. t., an applicant or candidate for an office (very rare for candidatus; not in Cic.), Scip. Afric. ap. : e petitoribus non alios adjuvare aut ad honorem pati pervenire,: hic generosior Descendat in campum petitor,.—
Judicial t. t., a claimant, plaintiff, in private or civil suits (whereas he who prefers the complaint in a criminal case is termed accusator; class.): quis erat petitor? Fannius: quis reus? Flavius,: petitoris personam capere, accusatoris deponere,; et saep.—
A suitor, wooer (post-class.), App M. 4, p. 309 Oud.; Sen. Fragm. § 39 Haas; Cod. Th. 3, 7, 1; —
In late Lat.: MILITIAE,a recruiting officer,; ; .

senses: a male given name, equivalent to English Peter

(v. infra d.): eum petit litteris, ut ad Britanniam proficisceretur,; .—Hence, pĕtītum, i, n., a prayer, desire, request, entreaty, .—
Polit. t. t., to apply or solicit for an office, to be a candidate for office (different from ambire, to go about among the people to collect their votes, to canvass, which took place after the petitio): nemo est ex iis, qui nunc petunt, qui, etc.,: consulatum,: praeturam,; .—
To solicit a person, to seek to possess, to woo: libidine sic accensa (Sempronia) ut viros saepius peteret quam peteretur,: cum te tam multi peterent, tu me una petisti,: formosam quisque petit,: multi illam petiere,; cf.: quae tuus Vir petet, cave, ne neges; Ne petitum aliunde eat,.—
To endeavor to obtain or pursue, to seek, strive after any thing, : fugā salutem petere,: praedam pedibus,: gloriam,: eloquentiae principatum,: sanguinis profusio vel fortuita vel petita,intentional, designed, produced by artificial means,.—With inf.: bene vivere,: victricemque petunt dextrae conjungere dextram,; : conubiis natam sociare Latinis,: aliquem transfigere ferro,.—With ex and abl., over, in the case of: ex hostibus victoriam petere,: supplicium ex se, non victoriam peti,: imperium ex victis hostibus populum Romanum petere,.—
To fetch any thing: qui argentum petit,: cibum e flammā,: altius initium rei demonstrandae,: aliquid a Graecis,: a litteris exiguam doloris oblivionem,to obtain,: suspirium alte,to fetch a deep sigh,; cf.: latere petitus imo spiritus,; and: gemitus alto de corde petiti,: haec ex veteri memoriā petita,.—
To take, betake one's self to any thing: iter a Vibone Brundisium terrā petere contendi,: diversas vias,: alium cursum,to take another route,: aliam in partem petebant fugam,betook themselves to flight, fled,.—
To refer to, relate to (poet.): Trojanos haec monstra petunt,.
